newsitem.title: CANADA: CIBC criticizes effort to limit top salaries.
newsitem.headline: CIBC criticizes effort to limit top salaries.

text.p: Mindful of growing public criticism, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce on Thursday sought to deflect calls for bank executives' pay to be capped and criticism over soaring profits for the Canadian industry.

CIBC chief executive Al Flood told reporters after the company's annual meeting that his bank was also targeted by a shareholder activist who had tried to table a proxy motion to cap executives' salaries at two other banks.
Flood said CIBC rejected an attempt by the Quebec activist to table a proxy motion at its meeting. But he said the bank would respect "due process" governing such efforts.

Quebec's Superior Court ruled this week in favor of Montreal activist Yves Michaud who sought to force National Bank of Canada and Royal Bank of Canada to put resolutions on pay limits and the selection of board members to a shareholder vote. As a result of the ruling, the two banks will do so at their upcoming annual meetings.
But Flood said salary limits would hurt the bank's ability to recruit talented executives and would likely not receive widespread shareholder support anyway.
"It would place a company...at a disadvantage if you put artificial ranges around compensation," he said. "We can easily lose people in a brain drain just south of the border."

Flood said Michaud was a "modest" shareholder unfamiliar to bank executives when he submitted his proposal. Unclear what his motives were, CIBC "declined his invitation to join in our proxy statement on that basis," Flood said.

CIBC was not party to the Quebec lawsuit but, like other Canadian banks, it too is receiving unwelcome attention over its profits, which soared to C$1.3 billion in fiscal 1996 from C$904 million the previous year.
Flood earned a salary and bonus of C$2.6 million last year while John Hunkin, president of the CIBC Wood Gundy unit, earned C$4.9 million.
Profits at Canada's big six banks topped C$6 billion in 1996, smashing the previous year's C$5.2 billion record, and four banks, including CIBC, reported profits over C$1 billion.

During the annual meeting, CIBC chief financial officer John Doran stressed that the bank paid C$1.5 billion in taxes and government levies in fiscal 1996, saying the banking industry is one of the highest taxed in Canada.

Flood highlighted the industry's role in creating jobs and its contribution to the economy. Financial services companies directly employ 500,000 workers in Canada and account for one sixth of the country's gross domestic product, he said.
"People should know the facts. I think it is a good industry," Flood told reporters.
